title: Replying to @carlo_narvaezz #broadway #westend #angelsinamerica #thea...
transcript: So I don't know if you'll find this story as interesting as I do, but I've always wanted to tell it. Which is that I might be the only person who saw this Angels in America revival starring Nathan Lane and Andrew Garfield in the specific way that I did. Cause while most people saw Part 1 and part 2 either on the same day or in the same week, due to a strangely specific set of circumstances, I ended up seeing part 2 a full year after Part 1. And I had to jump through some hoops to do so. So I was at the very end of my study abroad program in London, and the first preview of Angels in America at the National Theatre happened to fall on the very last free evening I had before going home permanently. And it was such a lucky stroke of timing that I didn't even care that I would only get to see part 1. I figured, I'll take what I can get. Of course, I didn't know it was gonna go to Broadway later. I thought I had exactly one shot at it, so I was determined to take it. And I wasn't able to get tickets before they sold out, so I was gonna rely on rush tickets, or “day seats,” as they call them there. Problem was, they sell tickets in the morning. It would require me to be late to class. So I begged my Professor, if I could be excused to come late. I explained the situation, I was like, “it's angels in America. It's Andrew Garfield, it's Nathan Lane.” “This is my one opportunity, please.” And my teacher was like, “alright, sure.” It was such a close call, but I got one of the last rush tickets they sold that morning on the one day I could possibly go. Cut to a year later, it's playing on Broadway. Obviously, I feel a little silly for having put in so much effort to see part 1 in London. But hindsight is 20-20. I made the right call for the time. But it did put me in a tricky situation because I was determined to see part two, but for a variety of reasons, I didn't wanna rewatch part 1. But the ticketing system was such that the seats were often paired up across parts, so it wasn't actually all that straightforward to only see part 2. I had to go to the box office and have them explain to me how to time it just right to go on a day where I could get a rush ticket to only part 2 after they had unpaired the ticket. So even more hoops to jump through. But I made it happen, and it was glorious. But here's the kicker. While I might not have seen this production the way Marianne Elliott and the producers intended, it's actually how these plays were originally done. Because Millennium Approaches was produced first, separately from Perestroika, so some of the original audience members of these plays had to wait a year between parts, just like I did. So I like to joke that I got the real, authentic experience.
